The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide for launching a **Google Compute Engine** VM that has a high‑end NVIDIA GPU (the closest match to an RTX A6000 that’s actually offered by GCP) and boots from the official Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image.

> ⚠️ **Important note:**  
> Google Cloud doesn’t list an “RTX A6000” SKU in its public GPU catalog. The closest equivalent that’s available today is the **NVIDIA A100** (or you can pick a V100/T4 if you’re looking for something cheaper). If you absolutely need an RTX A6000, you’ll have to look at other providers (e.g., AWS, Azure) or contact GCP sales for a custom solution.

---

## 1️⃣ Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Set variables first (replace with your own values)
PROJECT="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-demo"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  # Machine type – choose one that supports GPUs (n1-standard-8 is a common choice)
  --machine-type="n1-standard-8" \
  # Add a single NVIDIA A100 GPU
  --accelerator="type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1" \
  # Allow the instance to use the GPU driver installation script
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
  # Boot disk – use the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image
  --boot-disk-size="50GB" \
  --image-family="ubuntu-2004-lts" \
  --image-project="ubuntu-os-cloud" \
  # Optional: expose SSH port so you can connect later
  --tags=http-server,https-server \
  # Optional: add a firewall rule to allow SSH
  --allow-unauthenticated
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU & memory allocation. Pick a type that supports GPUs (`n1`, `c2`, `a2`, …). |
| `--accelerator` | Adds a GPU. Format: `type=<GPU_TYPE>,count=<NUM>` |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Runs a shell script after the instance starts. We'll use this to install the NVIDIA drivers automatically. |
| `--image-family` / `--image-project` | Boots from the official Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image maintained by Google. |

#### Example `startup.sh` (to auto‑install drivers)

Create a file named `startup.sh` in the same directory as your command:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Install NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y wget gnupg
wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/cuda-ubuntu2004.pin
sudo mv cuda-ubuntu2004.pin /etc/apt/preferences.d/cuda-repository-pin-600
wget http://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/12.2.0/local_installers/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004-12-2-local_12.2.0-525.60.13-1_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i cuda-repo-ubuntu2004-12-2-local_12.2.0-525.60.13-1_amd64.deb
sudo cp /var/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004-12-2-local/*.pub /usr/share/keyrings/
sudo apt-key add /var/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004-12-2-local/*.pub
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y cuda-drivers
# Reboot to activate drivers
sudo reboot
```

Make sure the script is executable:

```bash
chmod +x startup.sh
```

When the instance finishes starting, the script will run, install the NVIDIA driver, and reboot the VM so the driver takes effect.

---

## 2️⃣ Using the REST API directly

If you prefer to hit the Compute Engine REST endpoint yourself (e.g., from a program), here’s the minimal JSON payload you’d POST to:

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/<PROJECT>/zones/<ZONE>/instances
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "<INSTANCE_NAME>",
  "machineType": "projects/<PROJECT>/zones/<ZONE>/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [{ "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    { "acceleratorCount": 1, "acceleratorType": "projects/<PROJECT>/zones/<ZONE>/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100" }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y cuda-drivers && sudo reboot"
      }
    ]
  },
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Replace `<PROJECT>`, `<ZONE>`, and `<INSTANCE_NAME>` with your actual project ID, zone, and desired instance name. The `startup-script` metadata item is the same simple script that installs the NVIDIA driver and reboots the VM.

---

## 3️⃣ After the instance is running

Once the VM comes back online:

1. **SSH into it** (via Cloud Console or `gcloud compute ssh <INSTANCE_NAME>`)  
   ```bash
   gcloud compute ssh "$INSTANCE_NAME" --zone="$ZONE"
   ```
2. Verify the GPU is visible:
   ```bash
   lspci | grep -i nvidia
   nvidia-smi
   ```
3. If you installed CUDA, check the version:
   ```bash
   nvcc --version
   ```

You now have a fully functional Ubuntu 20.04 VM with an NVIDIA A100 GPU ready for deep‑learning workloads, rendering, or any GPU‑intensive task.

---
